assessment.nobel_worthiness: Structural estimation of demand and industry dynamics is a methodological foundation of modern empirical IO, merger analysis, antitrust and productivity measurement. Random-coefficients demand (BLP), the Olley-Pakes production-function approach, and the Ericson-Pakes framework for dynamic industries are now standard tools. The impact on research practice and policy is broad and durable, and it extends into trade, health and macro.
assessment.attribution: Pakes is the central figure across demand, production-function and dynamic-game methods. Berry (BLP, with Levinsohn) and Bresnahan (the New Empirical Industrial Organization and early demand estimation in differentiated products) are the clearest co-contributors. Levinsohn, Benkard, Reiss and Levin are real contributors, but the three-person limit makes this the most defensible core. Reasonable people could swap Levinsohn for Bresnahan.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The key papers date from the 1980s to the early 2000s and have decades of confirmation and heavy use in applied work and in regulatory practice.
uncertainties: Choosing which three of the seven credited names; Levinsohn's role in BLP and Bresnahan's early role are hard to weigh against each other.
Whether the committee prefers a prize for methods and tools over one for substantive findings.
I have not independently verified citation counts.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The collateral-constraint mechanism of Kiyotaki-Moore (1997), in which asset prices and credit limits amplify and propagate shocks, is a core building block of modern macro-finance. It is widely used in DSGE models and in the analysis of the 2008 crisis. The topic is highly relevant and the framework is tractable and general.
assessment.attribution: Kiyotaki-Moore is a clean two-author attribution. Gertler and Gilchrist belong to the financial-accelerator strand with Bernanke, who shared the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, so adding them raises overlap and attribution issues. I keep the proposal to the two originators of the collateral-dynamics mechanism.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The theory dates from about 1997 and has been extensively applied and extended, with empirical validation in the post-2008 period.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2022 prize on financial intermediation and crises could reduce the perceived novelty.
Whether the committee would want Gertler included given the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist line.
Empirical identification of collateral channels is still contested.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Melitz (2003) heterogeneous-firm model changed how trade is analysed, with selection, reallocation and the gains from trade operating through firm productivity. It reoriented empirical and theoretical trade work and links to micro data. Helpman's contributions in trade theory, including firm heterogeneity and the earlier work with Krugman, are of great importance.
assessment.attribution: Melitz is the clear originator of the core model. Helpman has a broad record that spans several candidate lines (B021 and this one), and Redding is more recent and quantitatively oriented. The Krugman prize (2008) covered the earlier new trade theory, so the claim here rests on the firm-heterogeneity wave.
assessment.maturity: Fairly mature. More than two decades of validation and extension, though the wider impact on welfare measurement is still being assessed.
uncertainties: Whether Melitz alone, or Melitz with Helpman, is the stronger framing; Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum is relevant prior and parallel work not credited on this ballot entry.
Overlap with the 2008 prize.
Debate about the welfare implications of the model relative to simpler gravity models.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Nominal rigidities and the New Keynesian framework are the workhorse of modern monetary-policy analysis. Staggered contracts (Taylor 1980), Calvo pricing (1983), and the synthesis and normative policy theory (Woodford) shaped central-bank practice and inflation targeting, and the framework is used constantly in policy institutions.
assessment.attribution: This is a crowded field: Gali, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Gertler and Smets are also credited, and Rotemberg and Clarida-Gali-Gertler are relevant. Three seats force a choice among Calvo and Taylor (the origins of price and wage setting) and Woodford (the integrated theory). The attribution is contestable, which is the main drawback.
assessment.maturity: Mature. The intellectual core is 40 years old and the policy use is institutionalised. The Great Inflation episode of 2021-23 prompted some reassessment of the framework.
uncertainties: Attribution among many strong contributors.
Sensitivity to the post-2020 inflation episode and criticism of the framework.
Possible overlap with earlier prizes for macro policy and expectations (Lucas, Sargent-Sims, Kydland-Prescott).

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The task-based view of technology and the study of how trade and technology shocks reshape labour demand and wage inequality have been very influential. Katz-Murphy and Autor-Levy-Murnane on skill demand, and Autor-Dorn-Hanson on the China shock, shaped the public and academic debate on inequality and the effects of automation, and the topic is of central social relevance.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central to both the task framework and the China-shock work, and Katz to the skill-premium and supply-demand literature. Dorn and Hanson are strong contributors to the trade-shock part. The task framework overlaps with Acemoglu's 2024 prize area, which complicates novelty and credit sharing.
assessment.maturity: Reasonably mature, since the skill-premium work goes back to the 1990s and the China-shock work is from about 2013. Some conclusions are still being revisited.
uncertainties: Overlap with Acemoglu's work on technology and inequality.
Whether the China-shock results generalise and how robust the identification is.
Whether the contribution counts more as empirical documentation than as a conceptual discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The construction of long-run top-income series from tax data, and the documentation of the evolution of wealth and income concentration, transformed the field and the public debate. The data infrastructure (World Inequality Database) is a lasting contribution, and the topic has major social importance.
assessment.attribution: Piketty-Saez (2003) is the core measurement contribution. Zucman's offshore-wealth work is newer. The theoretical component, such as the r>g interpretation, is more contested, so the case rests on measurement and data.
assessment.maturity: Mature in measurement terms, about 20 years. The theoretical interpretation and the measurement of wealth shares remain debated.
uncertainties: Methodological disputes about the measurement of top wealth and income shares.
Whether the committee views the contribution as measurement and documentation versus a causal or theoretical discovery.
Perceived policy and political salience.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Hsieh-Klenow (2009) introduced a tractable approach to quantifying the effects of resource misallocation on aggregate TFP, and it is a very widely used framework in growth and development accounting. The question of why countries differ in income is first-order. The framework links micro data to aggregate outcomes.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow are the authors of the central paper, and Restuccia-Rogerson (2008) developed parallel ideas. Whether a three-person group including Restuccia would be more appropriate is a legitimate question. I propose the two core authors of the measurement approach.
assessment.maturity: Moderately mature, about 15-17 years. The measurement approach is widely used but has been criticised for sensitivity to measurement error and to model assumptions.
uncertainties: Robustness of the misallocation measures to measurement error and modelling choices.
Parallel contribution of Restuccia and Rogerson.
Overlap with the 2025 prize on growth and with the growth work of the 1990s and 2000s.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Population-scale administrative data have allowed measurement of intergenerational mobility, with geographic variation and neighbourhood effects. The work has made opportunity measurable and has influenced policy debates. Chetty's wider work (see also B015) is exceptionally productive and influential.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the clear leader. Hendren, Friedman and Katz are essential co-authors on the mobility and neighbourhood-effects papers, and the sharing of credit among them is hard to assess. The proposal of two names is a judgment call.
assessment.maturity: The least mature of my eight picks. The key results are from the 2010s, and long-run replication and the question of causality for neighbourhood effects are still being worked out.
uncertainties: Time for the findings to be confirmed and for the lasting influence on theory to emerge.
Credit allocation among Chetty, Hendren, Friedman and Katz.
The conceptual contribution is partly data and measurement, as in B030.
